consequences: If important information is added to a resource or to certain parts of it, we consider the information as annotation. In terms of video, an annotation is anchored as an event in the temporal layout. An event can be related to a point in time or a time range within the temporal layout. According to the spatial extent video annotations can also correspond to a spatial position or space in a layer on top of the video. If an annotation is anchored in both time and space we refer to it as a spatio-temporal annotation. Adding layers of annotations to a video does not affect the video itself and therefore makes it possible to reuse it. However, there are several ways to extend a video. Basically the spatial and temporal dimensions are extensible by adding [Simultaneous Media](/patterns/view/Simultaneous-Media) such as presentation slides. The video frame itself can be augmented with further information layers to accomplish [Overlays](/patterns/view/Overlays) such as [Visual Highlighting](/patterns/view/Visual-Highlighting) or [Closed Captions](/patterns/view/Closed-Captions). Another purpose of annotations is the addition of navigational aids like [Hyperlinks](/patterns/view/Hyperlinks), [Table of Content](/patterns/view/Table-of-Content) or [Temporal Tags](/patterns/view/Temporal-Tags). Hence, it supports the searchability by relating semantics with time-related content. Annotations are further useful to communicate and discuss content-related issues with other users (e.g. [Comments](/patterns/view/Comments)). In educational settings annotations have been used to analyze video-captured situations like sports trainers at work (e.g. (Vohle2014)) or healthcare-related communication between doctors and patients. Annotations are not restricted to a certain type of media. Although text might be most commonly images, audio, video ([Add Video](/patterns/view/Add-Video)), or complex contents like web pages or maps are also feasible. While access rights for video playback are granted by default editing requires a more sophisticated rights management. For some people it might be permissible to add certain types of annotations that others might be allowed to read, edit, or delete. This can go along with a shift between the roles of the producer and consumer of instructional resources. Quality and quantity of the contributions may have to be monitored or moderated. Certain types of annotations are typically added by the instructor as part of the content preparation. For instance, a teacher anchors presentation slides ([Simultaneous Media](/patterns/Simultaneous-Media)) to a previously captured talk and defines a [Table of Contents](/patterns/view/Table-of-Content) as well as a short quiz ([Assessment](/patterns/view/Assessment)) every few minutes of the playback time. Problems can arise when a video gets heavily annotated. In the case of too many [Overlays](/patterns/view/Overlays), the video itself fades into the background. Even when further information is presented simultaneously, a split attention effect can cause cognitive overload (Clark2006). Beside that it becomes difficult to overview the temporal structure of the annotated content. Therefore an [Annotated Timeline](/patterns/view/Annotated-Timeline) could be helpful if annotations are distinguished by certain criteria in the way of [Classified marks](/patterns/view/Classified-Marks). From the chronological order it is not obvious who has added what annotation at what time. Therefore a possibility to [Follow Revisions](/patterns/view/Follow-Revisions) can help to unfold the editing process in order to comprehend or participate.
context: A learning environment is not closed, but rather open for contributions made by teachers and students.

evidence.rational: The \textit{MediaWiki} Extension \textit{Vi-Wiki} enables a collaborative way to annotate spatio-temporal hyperlinks to videos inside a wikipage as well as in the creole markup editor \protect[Seidel2012e].
Annotate bubbles and links in a authoring environment called \textit{BubblePly}.
Annotated captions implemented by the use of \textit{popcorn.js}, see: \href{http://ryersonssh500.com/}{http://ryersonssh500.com/}.

forces: Videos are comparatively large media files that need to be re-encoded after every editing session. A video can be considered as a self-contained media element that can include all other symbol systems like images, text, sound, and speech (Wetzel1994). Video cannot be changed without using tools that are capable of re-encoding the results into a suitable video format. Hence, a typical editing process requires much time, memory, and computational power. The result is an irreversible change of the original content. Furthermore, the resulting content is not comprised by [Search](/patterns/view/Search). One way to deal with that is to split up large files in order to get small files that are easier and faster to edit. Small units can be lined up and extended with other material in terms of [Sequential Media](/patterns/view/Sequential-Media). In an extreme case an audio file synchronized with an animated stream of different content types would remain as a type of [Simultaneous Media](/patterns/view/Simultaneous-Media).
name: Annotations
problem: Compared to text or images, it is difficult to modify a video file. Videos are technically self-contained, which implies their use as a broadcast medium in terms of teaching and learning. The involved people are impeded from making contributions or additions that are directly related to the time-based information structure.
solution: Make video extensible for the user through spatial and temporal annotations. Place them on top or beside the video.
synopsis: Extend video content without editing the video itself.

consequences: The optimal frame size can be easily detected by the layout space that is dedicated for the video.In constrast to common display sizes it is challenging to estimate current network capacities.  Providing flexible video formats, qualities and sizes requires enough capacity to store and to produce them imideatly after a user has added video content ([Add Content](/patterns/Add Content)).
context: The file size as well as the experienced image quality of a video is determined by the product of the pixels per frame, their colour depth, and the frame rate. When delivering web video there is a trade-off between fast delivery and the quality of the audiovisual content. This is determined by the individual system and network capabilities of the user

evidence.rational: The German news show \textit{Tagesschau} provides three quality levels (low, medium, high) and two different player formats (flash and HTML5). The the most appropriate option is set by default.
By default YouTube always chooses the best quality for the connection and player size.

forces: The frame size of video can be scaled to nearly every size of display. Down scaling is necessary to render large size video for small displays devices. As a result much more data is going to be transfered then that is needed for display. It is a wast of resources. In contrast up sclaing the frame size as part of a fluid web page layout or in [Full Screen](/patterns/Full Screen) mode can be borne by the image quality if interpolation lacks insufficent frame data. In both cases the data transfer capacity has an influences on the viewing experience. An insufficent transfer capacity interrupts playback while free capacities could be used to provided a better video quality. If a delay in delivery is unavoidable (e.g. due a changing connection speed) the user requires a feedback like a [loading indicator](/patterns/loading indicator). Beside that web browsers support only certain video formats. It seems clear to only deliver a suitable format considering video quality and particular advantages of it playback, e.g. for time-accurate navigation by using a [Table of content](/patterns/Table of content).
name: Appropriate Delivery
problem: While users expect a fast delivery of a high-quality video they would be overwhelmed in finding the optimal way of content delivery.
solution: Automatically deliver an appropriate video of maximum frame size and quality in a supported format that does not conflict with the possible data transfer capacity. Therefore provide several instances of the video that correlate with common screen resolutions, supported video formats, and network delivery capacities.
synopsis: Maxmize video quality and frame size automatically.

consequences:
Submitting an answer should not be mandatory, because the user can have other reasons for watch-     
ing or browsing the video. For instance, one might search for a topic she is interested in or on might     
watch it a second or third time.     
Further more, every learner should have a chance for learning. Excluding video segments or subse-     
quent assessment tasks because of a bad test result would compromise these chances. In contrast to     
that, thresholds are suitable for video-based serious games and explorative learning designs.     
Integrated questions can interfere the viewing experience and the learning progress. Therefore, the     
number of questions should be limited to one question per 5 minutes of playback. If there are more     
questions it is better to present them as ON - DEMAND TASKS .     
Once a questions has been integrated into the temporal structure of the video the corresponding     
answering options can be presented at the same time or separately from the question (SEPARATE     
QUESTION /ANSWER ). Multiple answering options of one question can be distributed over the playback     
time (Distributed Answers).
context: A video consists of several content units that are build on each other. A key concept is explained in the video that students need to understand before continuing the video
name: Assessment
problem: Learners tend to continue watching a video even if they did not understand the previous content section. With a lack of understanding, it becomes more and more difficult to comprehend the subsequent contents.
related: Seidel, N.: Video Assessment Patterns: Designing Video Player for Integrated Assessment. Proceedings of the 21st European Conference on Pattern Languages of Programs. p. 32:1--32:20. ACM, New York, NY, USA (2016).
solution: Pause the video after a key concept has been explained. Present a question as a little challenge that is suitable to determine how well the student understood the previous section. Since we focus on self-assessment it is important to provide immediate feedback including the correct solution. Neither make the submission of an answer mandatory nor define its result as a threshold for continuing the playback.
synopsis: Assessment of training success during the video presentation.

consequences:
The core functions of a video player define the minimum of what is necessary for using instructional videos. This set of control elements can be found in almost every video player. Even all web servers that are capable of HTML5 video incorporates these controls, which makes it easy to adopt them. See a list of the basic controls:           
          
 *   The **play and pause** button is necessary to start the video and control its playback.          
          
 *   A  **timeline** we need for navigation within the video and to estimate the playback time relative to the over-all duration. Without it we would need to wait until a requested scene comes up.          
          
 *   Adjustable  **volume controls** consider special needs of the user as well as of the surrounding physical environment that effects hearing.           
          
 *   Enable a  **full screen** presentation fades out extraneous information and puts a focus on the video content. Even thes basic controls only appear on request (e.g. mouse movement).          
          
On the one side these four elements don't overwhelme the user by a complex user interface interface, on the other side a basic video play like this does not support the usage and access of videographic learning resources.   In case the presentation of audio is not available or not audible the user can draw on  [Closed Captions](/patterns/Closed Captions) or a [Transcript](/patterns/Transcript) of the audio stream.A magnifier in terms of a  [Zoom](/patterns/Zoom) is suitable if the visual display is even in [Full Screen](/patterns/Full Screen) mode is experienced as too small.The navigation along the playback time can be cumbersome if the user tries to go to a exact position in time. At least by the use of [Temporal Bookmarks](/patterns/Temporal Bookmarks), a [Table of Content](/patterns/Table of Content) or [Temporal Tags](/patterns/Temporal Tags) frequently accessed scenes can be retrieved. A [Annotated Timeline](/patterns/Annotated Timeline) provides further aid to access [Annotations](/patterns/Annotations). Beside retrieving these fixed temporal positions everything in-between becomes could be played back faster or slower by adjusting the [Playback Speed](/patterns/Playback Speed). To [Skip Back](/patterns/Skip Back) a few seconds sometimes helps in order to repeat a part of a sentence or a few frames of an animation.
context: An application is dedicated to deliver the content of a video to the user

evidence.rational: Built-in video player of typical web browsers: a) Mozilla Firefox, b) Chromium, c) Internet Explorer, and d) Opera.

name: Basic Controls
problem: How to control the audiovisual presentation of a video?
solution: Every video player needs to provide basic control elements regarding the playback (play / pause), temporal navigation (skip, timeline), display mode (normal view / full screen), and volume control.
synopsis: Players provide basic control elements regarding the playback, temporal navigation, display mode, and volume control.

consequences:
A limited number of categories is attached to each type of annotation. When annotating a position in time the user needs to select one of the available categories. The categories are predefined by the instructional designer. They are not meant as a replacement of the annotation itself. All types of [Annotations](/patterns/view/Annotations) can be classified, e.g.:           
           
 *   Notices can be classified by their visibility / accessibility (private, group-wide or public).           
           
 *   [Temporal Tags](/patterns/view/Temporal-Tags) can be distinguished into geographical locations, persons, time ranges (e.g. 1960-1975), terms/definitions or by their top-level category.           
           
 *   A [Table of Content](/patterns/view/Table-of-Content) might be structured by its parts, e.g. introduction, methods, results, conclusion, references; or by didactic categories like learning goals, prior knowledge, definitions, examples.           
           
 *   [Hyperlinks](/patterns/view/Hyperlinks) can be (automatically) distinguished by their link target that may be an external resource, another video or lay within the same video.           
         
Not just instructors or course moderators but also learners can get a brief overview of all annotations and their relevance when they are sorted by category.         
A classification involves an increased semantic expressiveness. It represents an advantage for a better access to information and for didactic analysis.         
Unlike [User Traces](/patterns/view/User-Traces) the cumulated marked categories on the timeline do not represent the perception patterns but the distribution of the categories itself.         
If the number of annotations of a certain category exceeds the perceivable amount of data, other display methods need to be applied in order to represent the temporal layout. So classified annotations do not necessarily need to be mapped on an [Annotated Timeline](/patterns/view/Annotated-Timeline) they could also be placed beside the video.        
Nevertheless making a distinction between categories should not be experienced as a further barrier to contribute to annotations.
context: A large number of time-accurate annotations of the same type have been added to a video.

evidence.rational: \protect[Vohle2013] utilises traffic lights to indicate successful or adverse situations in video-captured presentations. In another application users were asked to mark critical parts in an eLecture for a real-life discussion in classroom later on.

Learners label critical situations as part of their apprenticeship to become driving instructors \protect[Vohle2010]. In that case the colours of traffic lights are used to indicate how critical the occurring situation is\protect\footnotemark.
Authoring of structured anchored annotations in a eLecture environment. Annotations can be classified in questions, comments or new topics \protect[Lauer2005].

example_description: So far citeN{Vohle2013} applied classification systems to [Comments](/patterns/view/Comments). When writing a comment the users can be asked to indicate the level of difficulty, their emotions or the perceived quality of the presented video scene. citeN{Trahasch2006,Lauer2005} implemented structured anchored discussion in eLectures whose contributions were classified by types like question, answer, explanation, suggestion or clarification.
forces: Annotations are already distinguished by their purpose, e.g. structuring the content ([Table of Content](/patterns/view/Table-of-Content), [Temporal Tags](/patterns/view/Temporal-Tags)), building relations ([Hyperlinks](/patterns/view/Hyperlinks)), contribute information ([Comments](/patterns/view/Comments)). Annotations of the same type seem to be more similar then they actually are.For instance comments: The nature of a comment can have different meanings. Someone might put a question in it while others make remarks or give a detailed explanation to the presented video content. Those who would like to answer questions or search for explanations would be overwhelmed if the total number of indistinguishable comments is too large. The identical appearance of annotations of a certain type suggests that their particular content is rather similar then different. But this is not necessarily the case and obstructive for surveying or accessing the information.
name: Classified Marks
problem: Viewers get confused by a large number of indistinguishable annotations and tend to miss the important ones.
solution: Therefore, find a meaningful classification scheme that helps the user to distinguish and filter different annotation. Such a scheme could rely on the type (e.g. comment, hyperlink, quiz), the content (e.g. question, remark, and mistake for annotated comments), relevance or ratings (e.g. green, yellow, red)
synopsis: Distinguish the quality of a large number of time-related marks.

consequences:
The availability of closed caption opens three different ways to perceive the content: the video without captions, the video with the captions, and the captions itself as an alternative representation of the audible contents. Providing diverse entry points can help to improve the video accessibility for different target groups. For impaired users who are deaf or hard of hearing, captions are essential in order to be able to comprehend and understand. But also non-impaired people can benefit from the written representation, e.g. to capture difficult terms, spellings or a foreign-language speech. This practice correlates with the modality principle of citeN{Mayer2009}. The principle states that words should be presented as speech rather than on-screen text, if learners have sufficient competencies and abilities to understand the spoken words.         
Because videos are often dedicated to a diverse audience with different language competencies and abilities, it is advisable to provide captions that can be turned on and off. Since closed captions are a special type of [Overlays](/patterns/view/Overlays), the user can hide or close them. That's why we call them "closed captions" in contrast to "open captions" or subtitles that are visible all the time.         
        
Captions consist of a synchronized text as an equivalent of spoken words and dialogues. Thus, the contained information is more detailed and precise, compared to other descriptions or meta data.          
Technically, captions are separate from the video file, which makes them flexible and exchangeable. Hence, it is possible to declare multiple caption files to cover different languages. Furthermore, they can be accessed by screen readers. Various data formats like *W3C Timed Text*, *QTtext/QuickTime text*, *SubViewer*,  and *SubRip are commonly used while none of them gained acceptance as a standard for video players.          
         
Captions should always be presented as in sync with the corresponding auditory information as possible.         
In terms of the amount of words and the frequency of changing subtitles, reading it all can become a challenging task for the user. Since space is limited, citeN{Brookes2000} recommends to show no more than 15 words at a time. For that reason common words can be abbreviated. In case of coincidental complex visual information and/or difficult subtitle contents, users should be allowed to reduce the [Playbacl Speed](/patterns/view/Playback-Speed). Alternatively, a [Transcript](/patterns/view/Transcript) can be read while the video is paused.         
To afford an appropriate readability against the background image, the font size, color/contrast, and position of the subtitles should be customizable. Adding a ticker border and shadow to the font brings further clarity. A simple font should be preferred to support readability. Sometimes different text colors are used to identify who is speaking.         
        
In case a video is completed by a simultaneous text-based media representation ([Simultaneous Media](/patterns/view/Simultaneous-Media)) like slides, it is unfavorable to add another visual information source for risk of a cognitive overload. The split-attention effect of concurring visual information sources can be seen as the main cognitive disadvantage of captions.        
        
Closed captions hardly include all auditory information. Text equivalents of acoustic events like noise, music or intonations are often excluded to express the spoken words. In the following example, the speaker is set at the beginning of the line, while the acoustic event follows within square brackets:         
        
    JACK: I got the machine ready. [engine starting]        
        
Providing comprehensive context information may support the understanding, but requires the user to read a lot more. Instead, a [Transcript](/patterns/view/Transcript) is a more suitable representation for details like this.        
        
Transcribing a video precisely requires much effort and time. Although automatic speech-recognition provided some advances, in most cases a video needs to be transcribed manually. A good authoring tool similar to [User Notes](/patterns/view/User-Notes) can help save time. Alternatively, the task can be outsourced to volunteers or companies who are offering such services.
context: An instructional video is usually accompanied by spoken word in a certain language

evidence.rational: \textit{edX} provide closed captions for the videos included in their Massive Open Online Courses.

\textit{Amara} is an advanced tool to annotated video subtitles in different languages. The creation process consists of three steps: 1) select video URL as well as source and target language, 2) type what you hear by the help of keyboard shortcuts, 3) synchronize the lines to its exact positions, 4) review the captions and publish it including a translation for the title and an abstract.
\textit{Dailymotion} provides a multi-track interface to annotate subtitles/caption in several languages. It is also possible to import and export srt-files.

forces:
For individuals that are deaf or hard of hearing, the audible cognitive channel of a video is not or only partly available. Besides the visual information, meta data is considered as a source of information for these target groups. [Table of Content](/patterns/view/Table-of-Content), [Temporal Tags](/patterns/view/Temporal-Tags) or an abstract in the [Video Manager](/patterns/view/Video-Manager) as well as other textual [Annotations](/patterns/view/Annotations) can help to get an overview of the learning content. However, meta  data lacks detailed information.         
        
If the volume is too low, it can be increased to some extent by using the volume controls ([Basic Controls](/patterns/view/Basic-Controls)). In noisy environments or in situations where listening to sound is unfavorable (e.g. in a open space office), audio cannot be played loud enough for sufficient comprehension without using headphones. Often, there is also no alternative to videos with low quality audio.        
        
Difficulties in understanding that are caused by a high speaking rate can be approached by reducing the [Playback Speed](/patterns/view/Playback-Speed).         
        
If you can only listen to the audio, it can be hard to extract the spelling of words, names or technical terms. To lower these language barriers, phrases can be displayed simultaneously with the video, e.g on slides or pictures. But these  ([Simultaneous Media](/patterns/view/Simultaneous-Media)) elements cover only a subset of the overall sum of spoken words. Especially context information as well as grammatical structures get lost, which is awkward for language learners. Furthermore, it is not always affordable, technically, to present information besides the video (e.g. on small display devices).
name: Closed Captions
problem: Audio information in a video can not be understood by audiences that are deaf, hard of hearing, or that have insufficient language competencies. These audiences are hardly able to participate in learning
solution: Support comprehension by providing closed captions of transcribed speech and other relevant audiovisual information. Let the user decide whether the subtitles should be visible or not. If they are visible they should be displayed inside the video frame.
synopsis: Present dialogues and relevant audio information as closed caption.

context: The video is delivered like broadcast media
name: Comments
problem: When watching an instructional video one might have questions, a remark or the will to  start a discussion. In typical broadcast media, users can not express themselves while the content providers don't notice user feedback.
solution: Let users anchor comments related to specific points in time. Also, enable re-comments to enable discussions. Do not restrict the form or style of the comments.
synopsis: Time-accurate comments that can emerge to anchored discussions.

consequences:
A revision history or revision log is a core function of collaborative writing tools but it is also important when changing video-related contents such as [Annotations](/patterns/view/Annotations). Whether users change a video including its annotations in an asynchronous or synchronous manner, the sequence of individual changes is crucial to make comparisons, revert to previous editions, or to branch a new version off the existing one.               
Thus revision logs can be a starting point for collaborative learning activities, because users can find out what their peers contributed to an assignment. For instance, it can be relevant to know who appended a section to the video in order to ask someone a question or to make additions.                 
Users can compare all different versions of a document to see which user applied what changes at what time. By that means revision logs are an important source to reconstruct and analyze collaborative learning activities. Logs can help the instructor to provide feedback or to grade the results of a group.                
               
In terms of [Remix](/patterns/view/Remix)ing an annotated video, each point in a revision log can be considered as a possible starting point for a new branch from the same source.                  
A comprehensive revision log needs to express different editing processes whether they result in changes of visual, audio, and text content or the overall content structure (e.g. changes in the sequence of concatenated videos). The following Table gives an overview about possible change operations that should be considered and represented in a revision log.               
               
If student activities become visible and comparable privacy concerns can arise. The captured data of an editing process tells a lot about personal working habits and the way of interacting with peers and the content. Most notably the user should be informed about what data is collected for what purpose. Whatever data it might be, it should not be used or analyzed to the disfavor of the students.                
                
Possible operations to make changes on content types like video, annotations or sequences of multiple videos similar to [Sequential Media](/patterns/view/Sequential Media):               
      
| **Properties**  | **Video**   | **Annotations**  | **Video Sequence** |      
| ------------- |-------------| -----| -----|      
| *existence* | add or remove | add or remove |  add or remove sequence |      
| *content*  |  source file | e.g. text, image, target link | include or remove element |            
| *time* | offset, end, exclude parts | temporal position and dimension within the playback time | sort order of elements |     
| *space* | spatial position and dimensions | spatial position and dimensions within the video frame| - |     
| *other* | e.g. video/audio effects | e.g. presentation | - |     
    
    
Since logs can get very long and exhaustive it is recommended to reserve sufficient space (e.g. one separate revision page per video). To allow further analysis, different data representations for export should be taken into account. Because some users -- especially instructors that provided the video and tasks -- want to stay informed about ongoing activities, system notification like email or RSS feeds can be considered.               
               
Although a revision log tells the user that a video file has changed, it is not said what contents exactly have been changed. Since differences need to be estimated by hand, the comparison can be supported by tools that highlight differences between two versions. The capabilities to automatically analyze visible differences between different versions of a video file become especially limited.
context: Students are encouraged to extend the instructional video with additional information. They do this by working individually or in small groups. Furthermore, the augmented content and the video itself can be manipulated and changed.

evidence.rational: \textit{PHP Melody} gives an basic example on how to present a log of basic activities such as uploading, rating, and following a video.
\textit{Advene} provides a basic represenation of a revision history by showing a chronological list of the previously created and edited annotations.

forces:
Since editing requires the user to watch the video, the recorded watching behavior could be taken as a first evidence for editing operations. To what extent parts of a video have been watched and used becomes visible in terms of [User Traces](/patterns/view/User-Traces) that are illustrated alongside the timeline. These user traces do not just correlate with editing operations, but also with the selection of the existing annotations as well as important or salient sections in the video. More generally, a [Viewing History](/patterns/view/Viewing-History} helps the user estimate which videos s/he has watched in the past sessions. This solution is limited to one user and a few sessions. Both of the latter solutions cover the level of perception but neither the contribution of additional content nor modifications of the content or presentation style.                
               
The following table provides an overview of operations that an individual can execute when working with a video, a video annotation or a sequence of videos. Modification of the video and its annotated artifact can be spread across different points in time. Determining these modifications in a video can be much more cumbersome then skimming a text or comparing two versions of an image. Furthermore, minor changes of visual objects are hard to identify.               
               
Keeping track with changes becomes important if a group of people is involved in the process of annotating ([Annotations](/patterns/view/Annotations)), editing or [Remix](/patterns/view/Remix)ing a video and its supplements.
name: Follow Revisions
problem: It is difficult to determine which parts of a video or which video annotations have been added, modified or removed since the last visit. If users are not able to identify these changes they may miss important contributions from other users.
solution: Implement comprehension of changes since the last visit. Provide a revision log that expresses different editing processes, whether they result in changes of visual, audio, and text content or the overall content structure (e.g. changes in the sequence of concatenated videos)
synopsis: Enable comprehension of changes since the last visit.

consequences: A learner should not be disadvantaged regarding the available learning resources when switching from normal presentation mode into full screen.Therefore any non-additional content that is synchronized to the video must be included in the full screen mode. Reasonable examples of these time-dependent resources are presentation slides ([Simultaneous Media](/patterns/Simultaneous Media)), [Overlays](/patterns/Overlays), [Visual Highlighting](/patterns/Visual Highlighting), and in-video assignments in terms of an [Assessment](/patterns/Assessment). Navigational elements that are normally presented inside the video frame need to be inherited in the full screen as well. This concerns all variants of [Hyperlinks](/patterns/Hyperlinks) (e.g. [Branching Videos](/patterns/Branching Videos) and [Detail on Demand](/patterns/Detail on Demand)). In that case [Related Videos](/patterns/Related Videos) can be shown when the playback has finished.On top of that are on demand interface elements. First of all [Basic Controls](/patterns/Basic Controls) including [Keyboard Commands](/patterns/Keyboard Commands) are irreplaceable to make use of audiovisual content. Additions to that depend on video properties. If it is a long video with structured learning contents a [Table of Content](/patterns/Table of Content) is essential. Fast moving images or a high level of detail can not do without [Playback Speed](/patterns/Playback Speed) or [Zoom](/patterns/Zoom).Regarding the purposed learning behaviour certain facilities to foster comprehension and communication should be taken into account. Then [Annotations](/patterns/Annotations) like [Comments](/patterns/Comments), [User Notes](/patterns/User Notes) should be spatially mapped on the [Annotated Timeline](/patterns/Annotated Timeline) as well.Whether to include [Closed Captions](/patterns/Closed Captions) or [Transcript](/patterns/Transcript) stands out of question in case there will be users with special need, even if they are no native speakers. In summary the mentioned components of a full screen presentation go beyond the built-in video-only full screen. To avoid naming confusions solutions like that are referred as  extit{couch mode}.
context: A video is enriched by further time-dependent resources such as synchronized slides,  extsc{Overlays} or  extsc{Annotations}.

evidence.rational: At the \textit{edX} MOOCs \textit{YouTube} videos can be extended by a transcript ("CC"). The essential control elements as well as a button the change the playback rate is shown on demand.
\textit{\textit{Arte.tv} has a "couch mode" that uses the entire browser window for video playback. Video within a channel can be sequentially browsed.}

\textit{\textit{Dailymotion Stream} is a full screen presentation of high quality videos that are arranged in a sequence. Users can skip through certain video channels or the stream of their previously watched videos. It is also possible to search other videos and browse the results in the \textit{Stream}. See \href{www.dailymotion.com/stream}{www.dailymotion.com/stream}.}

forces: Allowing a full screen presentation aims a bigger picture of the video frame. If the video has been enriched by time-depending [Overlays](/patterns/Overlays), [Annotations](/patterns/Annotations) or [Simultaneous Media](/patterns/view/SimultaneousMedia) important parts of the learning resources would be missing. In consequence the built-in full screen mode would is insufficient. On one side this could be also stated for the available navigational instruments such as [Basic Controls](/patterns/Basic Controls), [Table of Content](/patterns/Table of Content), [Search](/patterns/Search), [Comments](/patterns/Comments) or [Hyperlinks](/patterns/Hyperlinks). But on the other side full screen mode aims to maximise the viewing experience within a limited spatial space.
name: Full Screen
problem: Browsers built-in full-screen presentation of the video dismisses time-related contents and navigational instruments. So the user cannot see all relevant contents and has only limited possibilities to control and navigate the video.
solution: In full screen mode consider all contents that are related with the playback time of the video (e.g. synchronized slides). Also provide essential navigational elements such as 	extsc{Table of Content}, 	extsc{Hyperlinks} or buttons to turn [Closed Captions](/patterns/view/Closed-Captions) on or off.
synopsis: Include time-dependent media and essential controls on full screen.

consequences:
Many video players implement a set of core keyboard commands and touch gestures to provide [Basic Controls](/patterns/view/Basic-Controls). Especially blind people benefit from gestures since the graphical user interface is not accessible for them without a screen reader citep{Kane2011}.                
The shortcuts in Table                
ef{shortcut-table} could be identified in many different video players (see example), including *YouTube* as the most common one.                 
                
Typical commands and the assigned keyboard shortcuts and touch gestures:                
              
| **command** | **keyboard shortcut** | **touch gesture** |            
|---|---|---|              
|*play/pause the video* | space bar | double tap  |              
| *skip forward* | arrow right | drag to the right  |              
| *skip backward* | arrow left | drag to the left  |              
| *skip to 10% ... 90% of the playback time* | **1**-**9** | n.n. |               
| *skip to beginning* | **0** | n.n. |              
| *volume up* | arrow up | drag up  |              
| *volume down* | arrow down | drag down  |              
| *toggle full screen* | **F** | n.n. |               
| *exit full screen mode* | **Esc** | n.n.  |              
              
              
It is remarkable that the reading direction from left-to-right has become a universal standard for video players. Both the play button and the timeline are oriented to the right.                 
                
However, it is a challenging task to apply the recommendations for keyboard shortcuts and touch gestures on highly interactive video players. An [Annotated Timeline](/patterns/view/Annotated-Timeline) as well as an  extsc{Overlays} or other types of [Annotations](/patterns/view/Annotations) require complex interactions that are difficult to map on shortcuts.                 
                
In particular, it is  challenging to make keyboard shortcuts platform-independent, e.g for different web browsers and operating systems. Further conflicts can arise through the use of single key press commands. Especially if the user is required to enter text (e.g. [User Notes](/patterns/view/User-Notes), [Comments](/patterns/view/Comments) or [Assessment](/patterns/view/Assessment)) or the same key is already mapped as a common user-agent keyboard command.                 
                
Other interactive elements should be made accessible by the use of keystroke{~Tab~} and keystroke{~Enter~} only. Coding recommendations on how to do that are provided by the W3C citep{WAI-ARIA,WCAG2}                
Although the mentioned shortcuts might be very common, they need to be communicated to the user, e.g. on a help page.
context: Video players incorporate different designs and provide different user interfaces.

evidence.rational: The news cast \textit{Tagesschau} is based on \textit{Projekktor} player that supports common keyboard commands.
The video player is used for the interactive documentary \textit{CloudsOverCuba} covers the most common shortcuts including those to adjust playback speed.
\textit{Lernfunk / Opencast Matterhorn} is some kind of a negative example because they require the user to learn keyboard short cuts that are not common.

forces:
According to citeN{ShneidermanPlaisant2005}, it is crucial to consider the needs of diverse users from "novices to experts, age ranges, disabilities, and technological diversity" citep{ShneidermanPlaisant2005}.                      
Users who are blind, who have low vision or hand tremors find it difficult or impossible to make use of a video player that only provides a graphical user interface citep{WCAG2}. One reason for that is the non-standardized user interface facilitating [Basic Controls](/patterns/view/Basic-Controls) as well as additional controls (e.g. [Zoom](/patterns/view/Zoom) or [Skip Back](/patterns/view/Skip-Back)).

name: Shortcut Commands
problem: Graphical user interfaces are not accessible for the blind without a screen reader. These interfaces can also become frustrating for users who are not impaired in their vision, especially for frequently executed tasks.
solution: Enable keyboard shortcuts and touch gestures for the most frequent user interactions. Specifically, define those shortcuts that most of the video players have in common.
synopsis: Make the video player operable through a keyboard and touch interface.

context: The moving images of a video contain great visual details.
name: Loop
problem: Understanding a visual presented process or animation sometimes requires the user repeat the presentation multiple times in order to grasp all relevant details. Jumping back on timeline after every run is very cumbersome, especially if the requested scene is only a few seconds long.
solution: Therefore, enable the repetition of segments of a video. Inform the user when entering such a loop and provide a way to stop it
synopsis: Allow replay of the whole video or parts of it for repetition.

consequences: An indication of a delayed video delivery has become a standard since all major web browsers implemented it. Animated graphical control elements like a throbber, spinning wheels or progress bar visualize delays. Unlike progress bars the extent of a delay is not visualized. While a quantification would be desirable, the lack of reliable estimations would rather help then confuse the user concerning a delay. Estimating or predicting bandwidth capacity is often biased by slow start mechanisms, concurring data transfers, changing signal strength and many other aspects. When browsing interlinked videos it is necessary to reassure the user that a task like clicking a [Hyperlink](/patterns/Hyperlink) to open a video has been understood. Therefore a loading indicator shows that the computer is responding. Beside that the relative amount of loaded bytes is often visualized on the timeline ([Annotated Timeline](/patterns/Annotated Timeline)) in terms of a progress bar. Therefore a transmission problem becomes observable as the bar is not extending toward the right end of the timeline any more.Watching spinning wheel or a progress bar can help to improve the user experience. So fare only the video playback has been considered, while synchronizes learning contents ([Simultaneous Media](/patterns/Simultaneous Media)) such as slides may be as important for learning as the moving image and voice from the video.
context: Video browsing can be delayed by network latency, script execution and display problems.
forces: Video playback causes comparatively a high network traffic. Beside loading the surrounding web application it can take some time until playback could start. Usually the loading process becomes comprehensible through the growing page structure. After finishing the visible page load the video should be ready for playback or even start to play automatically. Otherwise the system state is getting inexplicable for the user. It could be that the video is still loading, but it is also possible that it does not exist or that it is not playable under the conditions of the browser.  Network delays caused by a bandwidth drop or lose can also be considered as situations where the extent of a task is unknown or the progress of the task cannot be determined by the user. A bandwidth drop can interrupt the video playback or prevent synchronized content from being loaded. Usually this is getting realized by the user because the audio and/or video presentation sticks. If there is incidentally no audio or if the image is static rather then moving the interruption is only recognizable at the timeline slider -- if its not hidden.Toggling the current quality of the video to a lower level is a possible work around to deal with bandwidth drops. Such [Appropriate Delivery](/patterns/Appropriate Delivery) mechanisms requires different versions of the same video of different qualities and frame sizes. If the lowest quality level is still above the current network capacities the video could be replaced by an audio presentation including a synchronized slides. Finally a [Transcript](/patterns/Transcript) may represent the learning content as an alternative.    However, if the network connection is totally broken the playback of unbuffered video content and the asynchroneous load of additional content terminates.
name: Loading Indicator
problem: User gets frustrated if the video player is not responding but remaining in an inexplicable state at start-up or during the playback.
solution: Immediately indicate a delay of data transmission or presentation not just for the video, but also for other attached resources (e.g. slides, images or parts of the web page)
synopsis: Provide feedback in case the media presentation is interrupted.

context: Video has a very high resolution or includes multiple camera angles (e.g. a multi-angle video).
name: Media Fragments
problem: Analysis and discussions that only related to a very small part of the video require the user frequently to navigate and zoom. User tasks that only relate to small area of the video   like an analysis or discussion  about visual details  focus
solution: Therefore, allow the user to extract a fragment of the video in order to work with this fragment. Provide handy tools to cut out parts of the video frame and to select a time range on the timeline
synopsis: Facilitate  the reuse and citation of video fragments.

consequences: In consequence the annotated content will be closely attached to its corresponding object inside the video frame. This solutions coincides with  extit{Gestalt Psychology}. Referring to the  extit{Law of Proximity} in someone's perception objects that are close to each other forming a group. According the  extif{Law of Common Movements} these objects are still considered as whole if they move simultaneously in the same direction. In case of a jiggling movement the position of the annotation should be eased in way that user can interact or make use of it. Otherwise a volatile [Annotation](/patterns/Annotation) is rather selectable nor readable.An object that disappears for a short time is another obstacle, e.g. when a walking woman passes a tree that hides her for a second. Therefore the re-positioning should be delayed to some extended to bridge the disappearance.Likewise challenging are multiple moving objects or a movable object and another static one. The existence of a single non-static spatio-temporal annotation can interfere or overlap other annotations. Thus it is recommended to limit the number of tracked objects to one if a collision with other can not be excluded.
context: An annotated video has been augmented with  extsc{Overlays} whose temporal and spatial position is related to a certain visual object in the video. This visual object can change its position over time

evidence.rational: [Asterpix](/patterns/Asterpix) was a start-up company combining object recognition or tracking with hypervideo technology. Detected objects in a video called beacons. They were displayed as little circles, following the object. The user could click on them to obtain further information or links to other resources including videos.
\textit{Advene} is an advanced video authoring tool that provides an object tracking feature among other implemented computer vision algorithms.

forces: Like almost of the spatial layout elements the position of [Annotations](/patterns/Annotations) is statically defined or inherited by the position of other page elements. However, videos are considered as self-containing elements but their moving images include distinguishable objects. Hence, these objects are moving within the video frame. Since spatial-temporal annotations inside the video ([Overlays](/patterns/Overlays)) are dedicated to augment the visual content with further informations they require a spatial proximity to the objects inside the video whether the objects move over time or not. When these spatial proximity is gone the annotation loses its context. It becomes an unrelated piece of information. [Visual Highlighting](/patterns/Visual Highlighting) certain object that are in focus of the narration would not make much sense if the object to be highlighted is not covered by the overlay. The same is true for spatially anchored [Hyperlinks](/patterns/Hyperlinks) that point to object-related content. If a link is not presented side by side with its corresponding object the link target is vaguely perceptible without a text label. A trivial way to deal with changing positions is to define multiple tuples containing the temporal and spatial position. As a consequence these tuples need to be identified as part of the authoring or annotation process. Not only the definition of complex movements would be cumbersome but also its maintenance.
name: Object Tracking
problem: The semantic relation of the annotation and its corresponding object in the video can not be ensured if they are not presented close to each other. Without this spatial context information an annotation can become meaningless. % Spatial proximity between a time-depending annotation and its semantically corresponding object in the video can not be ensured if the object is moving.
solution: Therefore, dynamically adjust the position of the annotation by analysing the movement of its corresponding object. Computer vision algorithm can be used for tracking the position of an object over time.
synopsis: Spatially attach annotations to moving objects in the video.

consequences:
Overlays define a visible area with a temporal and spatial position and dimension on top of the video frame. Within this area arbitrary contents can be displayed independent of the size of the display. Since overlays represent additional contents that can be added to the video we consider them a certain type of [Annotations](/patterns/view/Annotation).        
       
Variants of this solution lay the foundation for more specific patterns. These patterns can be classified in three types: 1) empty overlays that only emphasize existing contents (e.g. [Visual Highlighting](/patterns/view/Visual-Highlighting)); 2) overlays that serve as a link to related contents (e.g. [Hyperlinks](/patterns/view/Hyperlinks), [Detail on Demand](/patterns/view/Detail-on-Demand) or [Branching Video](/patterns/view/Branching-Videos)), and 3) overlays that contain all related information within themselves (e.g. [Closed Captions](/patterns/view/Closed-Captions) or some variants of [Assessment](/patterns/view/Assessment)).        
       
When using overlays there is tension between the quantity of displayed information and the area of the video frame that these contents require. The more content, the less parts of the video frame are visible. [Hyperlinks](/patterns/view/Hyperlinks) already address this problem by leading the user away in order to obtain another learning resource. But often one does not want the user to leave. Therefore, it is suitable to expand the size of the overlay until the purposed information can be presented inside. In that case the video should be paused as long the overlay is expanded.         
One of the strengths of overlays results from their spatial proximity to the corresponding contents or objects inside the video. This narrowness reinforces semantic relations. [Simultaneous Media](/patterns/view/Simultaneous-Media) presentations do not incorporate these connections (see cite{Kohler1975}). The spatial proximity of this anchored information saves space so it is even applicable on small display devices.       
       
Overlays should be positioned with care, especially if they overlap or hide relevant visual information. Since we are talking about moving images the position of overlays is not necessarily fixed. An overlay element can be positioned automatically depending on the visual object that it is attached to ([Object Tracking](/patterns/view/Object Tracking)).        
       
Overlays can lead to cognitive overload. For this reason the number of simultaneously visible overlays should be limited. Furthermore, users should have the chance to comprehend the video content and perceive all overlays as well as other time-dependent [Annotations](/patterns/view/Annotations) (e.g. [Simultaneous Media](/patterns/view/Simultaneous-Media) or [Comments](/patterns/view/Comments)). This should be possible without setting the [Playback Speed](/patterns/view/Playback-Speed) to a lower rate.       
       
The appearance of overlays can be annoying for users who would like to concentrate on the video content itself. Therefore, it should be possible to hide them individually or altogether.        
Sometimes overlays are intended to provide additional information that is unrelated to the visual or audio content of the video. In such cases an overlay informs the user at a certain point in time about the existence of related content. In order to achieve a consistent user interface these overlays should be placed at a fixed position at the margins of the video frame or even outside the video.       
       
Users cannot estimate for how long an overlay will be available for reading or clicking. Therefore it should be possible to return to the overlay after its disappearance. [Annotated Timeline](/patterns/view/Annotated-Timeline)s do not just provide an overview of temporally arranged events, but also a quick way to select single events such as overlays.
context: The instructor or students want to augment the video with further information. These additional contents can be synchronized with the video. The available space to present these contents is limited by the display size and the size of the video that is required to distinguish all necessary content.

evidence.rational: \textit{Edubreak} incorporates overlays in different situations. One of it is to highlight certain objects in the video. By selecting the overlay further information about the object becomes available. In the example above the movements of people playing table tennis has been analysed in order to encourage self reflection in sports.

forces:
Presenting additional contents beside the video in terms of [Simultaneous Media](/pattern/view/Simultaneous Media) requires sufficient space that could be better used by the video in terms of maximizing the frame size to make details visible.        
       
If the additional contents are to be presented in a sequential order, e.g. before or after the video as a way of [Sequential Media](/pattern/view/Sequential-Media), it would cause a destruction of semantic relation between particular items and the temporal and spatial position.
name: Overlays
problem: Displaying synchronized additional information beside the video reduces the available display size of the video.

related_patterns.description: Time-depending Hyperlinks are often presented inside the video frame.
related_patterns.label: Hyperlinks

solution: Present additional visual information in a time-dependent layer on top of the video. Make sure to place it closely to its corresponding visual contents. Avoid overlapping relevant visual information in the video
synopsis: Temporally present additional information on top of the video.

consequences:
If the user needs to follow critical steps the video can be slowed down. This is also useful if the user wants to take [User Notes](/patterns/view/User-Notes) or add [Annotations](/patterns/view/Annotations) during the playback. On the other hand instructions can be speeded up to get an overview or to move faster through sections of known content. Also trailers and screen credits can be processed faster. Nevertheless the timeline slider always corresponds to the playback speed by showing the movement within the temporal dimension. Instead of a fixed sequence and pace of information presentation the viewer's mental activities are less constrained by the author's choice on how to design the video [Schwan2004].      
      
Beside the benefit of slow motion and time lapse playback an adjustable playback speed enables visual and audible browsing and searching. By fast forward playback the user can get an overview of the visual contents and proceed until a scene of interest appears. In case the video is played within the range of normal and double playback rate it is even possible to listen and comprehend speech. Fast listening is an advantage over [Visual Summary](/patterns/view/Visual-Summary) techniques that aggregate key visual content as still images.[Simultaneous Media](/patterns/view/Simultaneous-Media) such as slides or pictures as well as [Overlays](/patterns/view/Overlays) and other time-depended contents are effected by changes of the playback rate. These elements can be dedicated for user interactions but become inaccessible at high playback rates.      
      
There is no common user interface metaphor representing playback speed controls. The pitching wheels as circular representation known from software DVD players can hardly be handled by correlating mouse or touch gestures. Sliders on the other hand are already stressed as timeline and volume control.
context: The presentation of video contents can result in the two extremes of a cognitive load. On the one hand, overload can be caused by fast scene changes or volatile details in visual dynamic processes. Mental underload, on the other hand, is related to almost unchanging images or irrelevant content

evidence.rational: \emph{MySpeed} is an extension for web browsers that allows the control of the presentation pace of Adobe Flash\texttrademark videos in the range of 0.3 and 3 \protect[MySpeed].
\emph{Cyber-Link} DVD player software \emph{PowerDVD} provides a wheel control around the play button to play videos up to two times slower and 16 times faster.
At \emph{YouTube} five discrete steps to adjust the playback speed can be selected.

example_description:
* citeN{Schwan2004} pointed out the cognitive benefits of interactive control over the playback speed in a user study. The participants learned from an instructional video how to tie nautical nodes.     
     
* A scientific prototype of citeN{Goldman2007} allows to go forward and backward in time when dragging the objects in the corresponding direction ootnote{See a demo at: href{http://vimeo.com/2345579?pg=embed&sec=2345579}{http://vimeo.com/2345579?pg=embed&sec=2345579}, lasted viewed: June 1st, 2014.}      
     
* At *Coursera* the presentation pace can be controlled by the + and - keys from 0.3 to double speed.     
     
* Since the time when VCR became popular, double arrows on the remote control were used to change the playback speed if pressed repeatedly.     
     
* *YouTube* offers, in the United States of America, five options to adjust the playback to 1/4, 1/2, Normal, 1.5x and 2x speed.     
     
* Modern web browsers provide an interface to adjust the *playbackRate* of HTML5 videos.
forces: Although a timeline slider ([Basic Controls](/patterns/view/Basic-Controls) and [Annotated Timeline](/patterns/view/Annotated-Timeline)) could be used to fast forward or backward it is difficult to keep a constant frame rate, particularly for short durations. The range in which the playback can be slowed down and speeded up is bound to the human ability of perception. The lower bound represents almost still images as far as the video compression and capturing frame rate allows it. The upper bound represents overspeeded image sequences those details, e.g. gestures and voice intonation are not noticeable any more.
name: Playback Speed
problem: The density of presented information in a video differs from the expected level of detail, sometimes it is perceived as too slow, sometimes as too fast.
solution: Integrate a mechanism to change the speed of presentation from slow motion to normal speed to time-lapse and vice versa.% as well as the direction of playback from forwards to backwards and vice versa
synopsis: Adjust playback speed and direction to your own cognitive needs.

consequences:
Simultaneous media presentations can be considered as an alternative for sequential or overlaid presentation of concurrent media artefacts ([Sequential Media](/patterns/view/Sequential-Media), [Overlays](/patterns/view/Overlays)). According to the "Temporal Contiguity Principle", stated by citeN{Mayer2009}, people learn better if corresponding words and pictures are presented simultaneously, rather than sequentially.       
Presentation slides are commonly used to transfer knowledge in a lecture, especially in higher education. Therefore, a simultaneous presentation of a lecture recording is often enriched with the simultaneous presentation of corresponding slides next to the video. This aims to simulate the situation of a lecturer standing and talking beside the slides.       
        
Apart from this example the content type for simultaneous presentations is not limited to slides or images. Also websites, [Synchronized Maps](/patterns/view/Synchronized-Maps) or even other videos such as screencasts as well as [Transcripts](/patterns/view/Transcripts) can be synchronized alongside the video. In some cases the primary video is even reduced to its audio channel to be synchronized with the previously video-captured static or interactive media elements.       
      
However, designers should pay attention to the accuracy to synchronize the involved media files. Otherwise, learners get distracted by unrelated audio and visual information.       
      
In a simultaneous presentation the video shares the available space with the concurrent media. Thus the size of the video frame decreases and its visual details become hardly perceptible. If visual details are essential for the comprehension the user can make use of the [Zoom](/patterns/view/Zoom) function.      
      
Semantic relations between the video content and simultaneously presented media items only arise from its synchronous appearance but not from it spatial proximity (see cite{Kohler1975}). This is the main difference to [Overlays](/patterns/view/Overlays) that benefit from spatial proximity. Thus, relevant relations need to be communicated by the narrator or by additional text labels.       
      
Users tend to split their attention between the video and the synchronized contents. This can be challenging in terms of the cognitive load if redundant information is presented as text and speech at the same time cite{Mayer2009,Homer2008}. Therefore short text should be preferred and displayed for a sufficient amount of time. On the other hand, non-native language speakers benefit from redundant text and speech. In each case the user should be able to adopt the presentation to its own pace ([Playback Speed](/patterns/view/Playback-Speed)) in order to process concurrent information. Users can also be enabled to deal with the possible effects of split attentions if they can decide whether a media stream should be displayed smaller, larger, or not at all.
context: Different types and formats of instructional media are provided to enable learning, whereas the given video contains the most important information.

evidence.rational: \textit{Metta.io} combines a video with text notes on top of a customized background image.
\textit{yovisto} provides a blend of overlayed and simultaneously displayed presentation slides on top of the video.

At \textit{openHPI} the \textit{Massive Open Online Courses} consist of videos of a lecturer and a synchronized stream of presentation slides aside. The portion of the screen width diservered for the one or the other media stream is adaptable by a slider.

forces:
Learning resources including the videos are often provided as separate files or online resources.  Because of the lack of [Hyperlinks](/patterns/view/Hyperlinks) relations between the video and supplemental contents are not explicit. The learner needs to identify and build these connections in order to understand the subject matter. Aligning the contents in a sequential order in terms of [Sequential Media](/patterns/view/Sequential-Media) does not emphasize elements that belong together. For instance, a lecturer video and the corresponding presentation slides could be watched in an arbitrary sequence, but the meaningful content relations are on the level of an individual slide and its corresponding video segment. Relations on the resource level, e.g. between two files or two web pages, are not accurate and therefore not sufficient for learning.       
      
In terms of linking essential, rather then additional, learning resources to a video, [Overlays](/patterns/view/Overlays) would either cover central parts of the video, or provide the resources only on demand (e.g. as a [Hyperlinks](/patterns/view/Hyperlink)).
name: Simultaneous Media
problem: A subject matter is not fully covered by the video, but provided with separate learning resources that are indispensable for learning. Despite the strong relations between the video and the other resources, they are stored and presented separately.
solution: Synchronize corresponding contents with segments of the video. Present them side by side to the video
synopsis: Prefer simultaneously rather then edged-in media.

consequences:
A table of contents provides quick access to time-related sections inside a video. Each section comprises a meaningful unit that is summarized in the section heading inside the table of contents. Therefore, users can get an overview of what the video is about. In the case of synchronous presented slides ([Simultaneous Media](/patterns/view/Simultaneous-Media)), the slide headlines often serve as items in the table of contents.            
            
Typical elements of a table of contents that can be found in many instructional videos are: introduction, main part, summary, and literature.            
This kind of structure is similar to advanced organizers that provide context and background information about the content. Alternatively citeN{Herron1994} provided chronological listed sentences representing particular scenes to facilitate students' listening comprehension of a video in a foreign language.             
            
In addition or as an alternative, preview images of the corresponding video scene are usable. It can be crucial to provide quick access to a videographic abstract in addition to a [Visual Summary](/patterns/view/)Visual-Summary) or further reading, such as making use of [Related Videos](/patterns/view/Related-Videos) or [Hyperlinks](/patterns/view/Hyperlinks).            
            
In contrast to [Temporal Tags](/patterns/view/Temporal-Tags) a table of contents is always ordered chronologically, but could be subjected to a hierarchical structure. More than two hierarchy levels are not recommended in order to maintain a neat arrangement. As a rule of thumb a table of contents should be visible without scrolling.              
            
Chapter marks are usually realized as hyperlinks referencing a media fragment cite{MediaFragmentURI}.            
            
However, unlike using a timeline slider, users are enabled to skip over a section or navigate directly to the beginning of a previously watched part of the video.              
            
Unlike [Temporal Tags](/patterns/view/Temporal-Tags), a chapter mark is only related to one point in time. While tags usually consist of one to three words, a chapter entry can be longer. For the sake of readability an entry should fit into one or two lines.
context: The video is longer then 20 Minutes. Its content stretches across several sections

evidence.rational: Inside the \textit{E-Learning Module on Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM)} a table of content is provided below the lecturer video while the slides appear on the right. (\href{http://www.iwrm-education.de/}{http://www.iwrm-education.de/}).
\textit{NPTEL} is an Indian university portal for lecture recordings that incorporates a nicely structured table of content.

\textit{Videolecture.net} provides a typical example of listed slide headings. In the screen shot above unfortunately slides with the same title got included. This redundancy might be a result of a automatically processing of presentation slides or a slide video.

forces:
The longer the video, the more difficult it gets to find and navigate to certain content sections precisely by using  the timeline slider. Even if temporal navigation is supported by a visual feedback tool (e.g. [Visual Summary](/patterns/view/Visual-Summary)), an adjustable  [Playback Speed](/patterns/view/Playback-Speed) or a button to [Skip Back](/patterns/view/Skip-Back), navigating on a timeline is a time-consuming task.            
            
[Annotations](/patterns/view/Annotations) such as [Temporal Tags](/patterns/view/Temporal-Tags), [User Notes](/patterns/view/User-Notes), or [Comments](/patterns/view/Comments) may help to overcome an insufficient content structure. However, these navigation aids are typically defined by the users (e.g. the learners) after the videos have been made available.            
            
Before watching a longer video it is useful to get an overview. It is not always the case that an overview is provided within the first minutes of a video or in terms of an written abstract as part of the [Video Manager](/patterns/view/Video-Manager). [Search](/patterns/view/Search)ing inside the video is a possible way to falsify the existence of assumed content. Furthermore, a [Visual Summary](/patterns/view/Visual-Summary) is far from able to represent the structure and essence of the spoken language.
name: Table of Content
problem: Content units of a video can be neither overviewed nor accessed precisely. So the user wastes time for searching and navigating.
solution: Provide a navigable table of content next to the video that provides a brief overview of the video content. Enable time accurate access to the corresponding content sections. Highlight the currently watched section in the table of content
synopsis: Chronologically ordered list to access content inside the video.

consequences:
"Transcripts allow deaf/blind users to process content through the use of refreshable Braille and other devices. Screen reader users may also prefer the transcript over listening to the audio of the web multimedia." cite{Brookes2000}      
In contrast to [Closed Captions](/patterns/view/Closed-Captions), other audible cues such as descriptions of music, noise or intonations are typically not included. Therefore, the written narration appears in a flow of paragraphs instead of time-dependent snipped dialogs. This enables the user to skim the text much quicker than listening to the narration at a higher rate. In the same way as non-impaired users would increase the [Playback Speed](/patterns/view/Playback-Speed), some screen reader users prefer to listen to the reader at a much higher rate. Thus, they can access a transcript much faster.       
      
The transcript text should be displayed stationarily rather than inside a scrolling panel that is tiring for the reader cite{Brookes2000}. citeN{Brookes2000} recommends at least 15 seconds for 50 words so that the user has time to look away from the display. Single words, sentences or paragraphs can be selected in order to navigate to the corresponding playback time. During the playback, the corresponding section of the transcript should be highlighted.       
       
Unlike a [Table of Content](/patterns/view/Table-of-Content) or an abstract in the [Video Manager](/patterns/view/Video-Manager), written transcripts provide not just an overview but also an accurate representation of the spoken words. Thus, a transcript is an additional representation of the provided video learning resource.       
      
In the same way, it facilitates searching and browsing for the user. Besides, it is a remarkable source to enable [Search](/patterns/view/Search) inside and across multiple videos.       
      
The presentation of a transcript requires sufficient space beside the video frame. This can be a problem on small display devices or in applications that include other time-related or time-dependent components, e.g. [Simultaneous Media](/patterns/view/Simultaneous-Media) in terms of presentation slides.      
Compared to [Closed Captions](/patterns/view/Closed-Captions), the effort to create transcripts containing all auditory information and their relation to the video is much higher. On the other hand, blind and deaf people derive a greater benefit from a self-containing text equivalent as opposed to in sync sentences, i. e. subtitles.      
Transcripts are usually not considered as user-generated content [Annotations](/patterns/view/Annotations) whereas [User Notes](/patterns/view/User-Notes) describe a way on how to achieve personal transcripts.       
      
Although users without special needs benefit from a transcript (e.g. to search inside the video) this type of [Simultaneous Media](/patterns/view/Simultaneous-Media) does not have to be visible all the time. In order to avoid a split attention effect, transcripts should be made available on demand.         
      
In case a video is completed by a simultaneous text-based media representation ([Simultaneous Media](/patterns/view/Simultaneous-Media)) it is unfavorable to add another visual information source for risk of a cognitive overload. The split-attention effect of concurring visual information sources can be seen as the main cognitive disadvantage of captions.

consequences:
The purpose of highlighting visual elements excludes interactions that are inherent to  [Overlays](/patterns/view/Overlays) in general and [Hyperlinks](/patterns/view/Hyperlinks) in particular.       
      
Visual highlighting can be derived from the *Signalling Principle* of the Theory of Multimedia Learning by citeN{Mayer2009}. Highlighting or marking draws attention to essential visual aspects of the presentation. It supports mental selection and organization during the perception of instructional videos. Ideally there should be only one element highlighted at a time. Therefore it can be seen as an analogy to real-life lessons where teachers point at objects with their fingers, a stick, or a laser pointer.       
It is an advantage if a part of a moving image calls somebody's attention while its context stays visible. The relationship between the parts and the whole carries a meaning beyond the spatial arrangement. [Zoom](/patterns/view/Zoom)ing is an alternative way to draw attention but it neglects this whole/part relationship.      
      
This method can also be applied in discussions among students who want to focus on spatial objects rather than on explaining their location verbally. Consequently instructors and students can make use of the possibility to highlight content elements.      
      
There are many possible ways to pay attention to an object in a video frame without manipulating the video itself. Technically it needs to be realized with a visual layer on top of the video. Colored frames or boxes can be put around the object in question, arrows can point at them, or the surrounding area can be grayed out. Highlighted elements should always appear distinguishable from their background. In a few cases it might be necessary to reinforce the visibility by blinking colors or animating appearing or disappearing overlays.      
      
If the highlighting is related to a moving object it becomes necessary to change its position accordingly. [Object Tracking](/patterns/view/Object-Tracking) algorithms can handle this to some extent. Annotation by hand becomes cumbersome if an object moves in a non-linear manner.      
      
However, highlighting certain objects interrupts the visual representation as a whole. In the same way as elements emerge from the background, the elements in the background do get less attention. That's why it is important to give the user enough time for viewing the whole picture before focusing upon a detail.

name: Branching Videos
problem: When watching a video learners are faced with different (content-driven) opportunities to leave the video. For instance, learners may want to close individual knowledge gaps or they may want to deepen a topic before or instead of continuing the playback. In this cases, they might not learn as much as they could if they continue the video.
