consequences:
In contrast to usual [Hyperlinks](/patterns/view/Hyperlinks) leading to another website or a position in time, this kind of link is dedicated to a certain sequence in a target video. If a user follows a detail on demand link the source video will halt while the target sequence starts playing. The playback can be aborted by following a return link back to the origin. If the playback is not aborted by the user it will automatically return to the origin when the dedicated sequence is completed (see Figure        
 above). This pattern is related with the *cycle* hypertext pattern that [Bernstein1998] identified in hyperfiction documents.Detail on demand gives the user the opportunity to comprehend further details that are necessary to understand the originated content. Such details could be a definition of a term or an explanation of a concept. While dealing with that details the surrounding context of the initial video is only one click away. Watching video sequences on demand is like zooming into a picture. The incorporated return behaviour to the initial video is like zooming out to get back to the whole picture again. Learners should not lose the indicated learning path when following a [Hyperlink](/patterns/view/Hyperlinks) to another video. The behaviour of automatically returning to the original video let the learners keep track. Therefore the linked sequences should not be too long. Nevertheless, links to additional videos can be offered as [Related Videos](/patterns/view/Related-Videos). Video-based details that have been requested on demand can also contain further links to on-demand content. Although loops can be avoided, a multilevel recursive decline and ascent, through aborting or terminating a sequence, makes it difficult to orient towards the original video. To avoid cognitive overload, the hierarchy of linked videos should not be beyond one or two levels. A [Journal Navigation](/patterns/view/Journaled-Navigation) can help to go back and forth in the navigation history. Überträgt man das Konzept von Hypertext auf Videos, lassen sich Querbeziehungen zu anderen Ressourcen herstellen. Gemäß der zeitabhängigen Informationsrepräsentation erscheinen auch Hyperlinks in Abhängigkeit der Wiedergabezeit. Man unterscheidet folgende Ausprägungen von Hyperlinks in zeitabhängigen Medien:        
        
 *   Temporal Links: Die Hyperlinks besitzen eine zeitliche Position (Startzeitpunkt) und Dimension (Anzeigedauer).        
        
 *   Spatial-temporal Links: Zusätzlich zu Eigenschaften von Temporal Links verfügen sie über einen räumlich abgegrenzten Link-Anker innerhalb des Video-Frames. Der Anker hat eine vertikale und horizontale Ausdehnung in Bezug zu einem Punkt innerhalb der Koordinaten des Video-Frames.        
        
 *   Zyklische Links: Diese Art von Link erlaubt nach der Linkaktivierung einen zeitgenauen Rücksprung vom Zielvideo zum Quellvideo.        
        
 *   Externe Links: Hyperlinks, deren Ziel außerhalb der Lernumgebung liegt.        
        
Für die Darstellung der Links gilt es einige Randbedingungen zu beachten. Bezieht sich ein Link auf ein Objekt im Video, sollte der Link in dessen Nähe erscheinen.Es ist davon abzuraten, bestimmte Objekte als Link-Anker mit dem Benutzer zu vereinbaren, da somit nur dann Links definiert werden können, wenn die vereinbarten Objekte im Video auftauchen. Darüberhinaus sollten dem Anwender die Konsequenzen der Linkaktivierung deutlich gemacht werden. Es ist ein Unterschied, ob der Link auf eine Ziel innerhalb des Videos, auf ein anderes Video der Seite oder gar auf eine externe Seite verweist. Empfehlenswert ist die Kennzeichnung des Links durch unterschiedliche Icons sowie ein Label, welches das Verweisziel genauer spezifiziert.

In case one might have identified a cross-relation between videos the relation remains implicit and not visible for other learners.
solution: Therefore, make content relations explicit by linking segments in one video with another video or learning resource. Distinguish visually, whether a link points to another video within the same environment or to any other external resource. When of referencing continuous media such as video or audio enable time-accurate link targets to address contents more precisely.
synopsis: Cross reference through time-related spatio-temporal links.

consequences:
A journaled navigation is comparable with the return button within a web browser that leads you not just to the previous page but also to the vertical page position. Transferred to the navigation in a video collection going back or forth in the browser history should therefore lead to the temporal position where the playback was interrupted at the last visit. This does not exclude a return to the beginning of the video. A transitions between the playback of different videos can be almost seamlessly when intelligent buffering strategies are taken into account. Instead of reloading all page content only the video and its related contents need to be updated.   
   
Offering a journaled navigation supports the use of sequential organized subsets of a video collection such as [Sequential Media](/patterns/Sequential-Media). In contrast to [Detail on Demand](/patterns/view/Detail-on-Demand) it is always the users choice to go back to a previous watched video, instead of getting automatically redirected to the source video when a sequence of the target video has ended.
context: Browsing from one video to another leaves a trace that is not just resource-related but also related to the viewed scenes of each video
example_description: As known so far, *YouTube*, *IWRM education* cite{Leidel2012}, *digital-tutors*, and *HyperActive* cite{Bove2000} provide examples for going back and forth in respect to the previous playback position. At *YouTube* the built-in browser buttons have to be used with the drawback of reloading the whole page instead of the video only.
forces: Browsing along the trace of previously requested resources is a frequently used feature of hypertext browsers that has not been widely adopted for video browsing yet.The XML Linking Language, as recommended by the W3 Consortium, incorporates bi-directional arcs between resources [xlink]. These arcs do not need to be defined manually because they can be derived as inverse of uni-directed links. Typically, browser histories allow the user to traverse a link in the opposite direction. A browser history includes a backward chronological list of resource identifiers and the time stamp when the resource was requested. Time-based media such as video is not attributed with temporal information of their origin or target. Therefore temporal [Hyperlinks](/patterns/view/Hyperlinks) and additional navigation aids are needed. From a didactically point of view content structures like [Pyramid](/patterns/Pyramid) or [Sequential Media](/patterns/view/Sequential-Media) relay on the ability to browse forth and back alongside a predefined learning path. As proposed for [Hyperlinks](/patterns/view/Hyperlinks) transitions between single videos should not interrupt the presentation flow.
name: Journaled Navigation
problem: Browsing between videos must be supported in both directions. While the forward directed links are commonly implemented, the way back is not considered.
solution: Provide journaled navigation to go smoothly and time-accurately back and forth in the sequence of watched videos. In addition to the 	extsc{Viewing History} and the browser history users should be able to recall the starting point of the previously watched segments.
synopsis: Time accuracy when going back and forth in a sequence of videos.

consequences:
For the ease of access, the user should to some extent be allowed to set his or her own content structure on top of the given one.      
The concept of playlists is known from music software or other media players. Also browser bookmarks can be considered as a user-generated list of playable items.       
Playlists help to organize personal learning activities within a large amount of audiovisual resources. But that does not exclude their use within a group of learners, no matter if the list is publicly accessible or not. Organizing a playlist outside the learning environment by collecting [Temporal Bookmarks](/patterns/view/Temporal-Bookmarks) is not an added value feature of the environment itself.       
The more items a playlist contains the more hierarchical or semantic structuring is recommended. That can be achieved through folders and subfolders (e.g. multiple playlists) as well as through personal notes or tags. Finally the possibility to bring the items in a user-defined order can be considered as a basic way to bring the items into a linear order. Playlist do not need to be stored persistently. When visitors do not need to register, playlist items can be stored until the end of the session.
context: Videos in a large collection are filed in a predefined category system.
forces:
The need for a personal organisation of learning activities and content can be derived from the number of videos and the amount of playback time. The more resources are available the more possible learning paths can be followed and the greater is the demand to organize it.  A personal organisation of learning resources incorporates different activities, e.g.:          
         
 *   Making a preselection of items when searching and browsing ([Search](/patterns/view/Search), [Video Manager](/patterns/view/Video Manager)).      
         
 *   Sorting or grouping resources of interest in a personal classification system (e.g. by topic).         
         
 *   Storing of organized content, at least for the time of use.         
         
 *   Sharing of the arranged content with peers.         
         
Unlike algorithmically assorted [Related Videos](/patterns/view/Related-Videos) the user's own choice of videos is a relevant demand. In contrast to [Temporal Bookmarks](/patterns/view/Temporal Bookmarks), the organized items refer to videos as a whole instead of specific parts of it. Apart from that, bookmarks are not necessarily stored within the learning environment.
name: Playlist
problem: When browsing a large collection of videos, users need to organize resources by their own needs. Selected, previously watched resources should not need to be searched over and over again.
solution: Provide learners a playlist, where they can collect and store subsets of a video collection for later use. These personal subsets can be freely extended or reduced by videos that are part of the learning environment
synopsis: Temporally select learning resources for later use.

consequences: Related items can be presented in a list or matrix. A single item contains at least a meaningful label and a link. Often meta data or a  [Visual Summary](/patterns/view/Visual-Summary) is displayed. The number of concurrent displayed items can vary from two to twelve. Further resources can be offered on demand.    To identify possible related material a broad range of algorithms can be found in literature. Typical approaches take resource-related as well as audience-related information into account. In contrast to determined learning paths as intended in [Sequential Media](/patterns/view/Sequential-Media) this pattern encourages the user to browse in a non-linear way. In a large collection where categorized or tagged items appear in a hardly manageable number the effort in using a [Video Manager](/patterns/view/Video-Manager) or [Search](/patterns/view/Search) can be reduced by automating the search and presentation of related videos for a quick access. Neither does the user have to chose the right search term nor does she or he has to browse through other items within the same category. Despite that related resources are presented in spatial proximity a temporal proximity in order to refer on prior knowledge should be achieved by [Detail on Demand](/patterns/view/Detail-on-Demand).
context: A set of videos that strongly build on each other in a sequential manner should be rather interlinked with each other or concatenated in the way of  extsc{Sequential Media}. Hence additional learning resources are not intended to provide a linear learning path. The content of a video bears many implicit ties to other learning resources. Learners can be motivated to follow these ties and consume resources that are part of the learning environment

evidence.rational: Paginated sequence of related videos at Dailymotion\protect\setcounter{footnote}{2}\protect\footnotemark[\value{footnote}].
Serendity browsing within related films on the website of the Franco-German TV network \emph{Arte}\protect\setcounter{footnote}{3}\protect\footnotemark[\value{footnote}] in 2012.
At \textit{YouTube} related videos are presented permanently in parallel to the video (right) and additionally after termination of playback inside the video frame (left).

forces: Similar resources are often tagged with the same keywords or filed within the same category. Therefore a [Video Manager](/patterns/view/Video-Manager) is suitable to identify similar items as long the category or tag hierarchy with its belonging items remains manageable. Otherwise a manual [Search](/patterns/view/Search) for keywords that might not have been tagged but extracted from slides, annotations or other meta data is required by the user.
name: Related Videos
problem: The desire to watch another video awakes during or after a video presentation. The viewer might be looking for another video during the playback if the one presented does not fulfil his/her needs. After completion, the viewer would like to continue with a subsequent or deepening lecture. In both cases, the learner should not leave the learning environment if he/she could proceed the learning with an appropriate resource.
solution: Always offer links to additional learning resources that fosters continued learning activities. Provide these links after one video has ended. In addition to that display a set of related videos beside the current video. Consider resources that are semantically or didactically related to the current video.
synopsis: Offer additional but related instructional videos.

context: Producing a video from scratch takes a lot of time. The same is true for video annotations  such as  extsc{Table of Content},  extsc{Hyperlinks} or  extsc{Assessment}. The video and its annotations can be modified or extended by other users
name: Remix
problem: To create a new video users cannot make use of existing parts of a video or video annotations
solution: Therefore, allow users to take an instance of a video including all its annotations as a starting point for their own version or remix of the original content. Make it possible to integrate or connect artefacts from different sources
synopsis: Existing arrangements of videos and annotations can be used as a starting point for individual remixes.

consequences: Bei der Erstellung eines zeitbezogenen Suchindexes kann man auf synchroniserte Medien (Folien, Bilder) ebenso zurückgreifen, wie auf zeitgenaue Schlüsselwörter und Annotationen (Kommentare, Notizen, Hyperlinks) der Nutzer. Man differenziert dabei zwischen Metainformationen, welche sich auf das gesamte Dokument beziehen und solchen, die mit zeitlichen Positionen in Verbindung stehen. Letztere können dabei kollaborativ ergänzt und verifiziert werden.Die Effektivität einer Suchfunktion wird nicht zuletzt durch die Repräsentation der Suchergebnisse bestimmt. name: Search
problem: Verbal information stored in a video is not accessible at a stroke. Increasing the playback rate or listening all speech takes to much time. Beside that, one may also have to look for written words that are part of the video and its synchronized media streams. In consequence, the verbal content related to a video can not be searched directly.
solution: Enable a search within all available sources that are related to the video. Consider video related meta data and all available media streams including audio. Take also information into account that needs to be extracted from annotated contents such as synchronized slides, images, tags, or links. Provide a link from each search result back to its corresponding artefact at a given playback time.
synopsis: Search within and across videos.

name: Temporal Bookmarks
problem: Time-related events or periods in the video are not part of a URL. If you are sharing a URL you cannot point to a certain moment or period in the video. This information needs to be transferred separately. Often it is missing or only verbally described. The one who would like to watch a particular scene has to open the link and navigate manually to the desired scene.
solution: Implement media fragments like time stamps, periods or section names as part of the URL. When opening a URL that includes these fragment identifiers parse them and navigate the video player to the given temporal position.
synopsis: Filling of references that allows accurate access to videos.

context: User have access to a comprehensive collection of videos. These videos can be organized by categories and tags.
name: User Ratings
problem: Users are overwhelmed of similar videos. Differences in quality or relevance can not be recognized at a glance. They cannot estimate which videos are worth to watch.
solution: Therefore, let users rate the videos regarding their quality or relevance. Show the rating results whenever users will have the choice to select one of many video, e.g. in a list of search results or category contents

name: Sequential Media
problem: If the video would be watched in a different order it would become difficult to comprehend them. Important prior knowledge (e.g. about term, concepts, theories) could be missing or the sequence of an explanation or a process order would be messed up.
solution: Therefore, sequence the videos in fixed order and make the order visible to the user. Provide a menu or enumerated list to emphasize the sequence of videos. Foster navigation between adjacent videos through direct links. Automatically load the subsequent video when a video ends
synopsis: Sequencing continuous and discrete media in a flow.

context: The video learning environment contains a collection of videos that might be organized by categories and tags.
name: Video Manager
problem: User can select videos from a list or menu. Because of a lack of sufficient information about the video content the user needs to open the videos one by one in order to find the desired one.
solution: Support browsing and searching by providing a meaningful overview of any set or subset of the videos in the system. Include necessary meta data (e.g. title, author, tags, description, duration, ratings) as well as a visual preview. Provide a direct link to the video player in order to start the playback
synopsis: Brief overview of multiple videos linked to detailed contents.

context: An uploaded video file has some failures, e.g. the image is too dark, it is wrong orientated or the first three seconds need to be trimmed

name: Video Manipulation
problem: If a video has been uploaded the file has to be used as is. For editing the file needs to be (1) downloaded, (2) opened in a video editing software, (3) edited and re-encoded, and (4) finally uploaded to the system again. For applying only minor changes this process is too time-consuming and reduces the quality because of the re-encoding.
solution: Enable basic editing tools that only manipulate the presentation and leave the file untouched. For example, one could adjust image properties like brightness, contrast, and colours by using filters. One might also need to change the orientation from landscape to portrait. Unwanted scenes can be excluded from playback instead of trimming or cutting the file
synopsis: Enable basic video manipulation for content production.

name: Viewing History
problem: The learner cannot exactly remember which videos they have already watched. Furthermore, they hardly remember what parts they have seen so far.
solution: Offer a viewing history that lists the previously watched videos. Make sure the user can estimate to what extent a video has been watched already
synopsis: Indicate the videos that have been watched in previous sessions.

consequences:
On the one hand the slider handle represents the playback position on the timeline and can be used to navigate back and forth. On the other hand the timeline obtains exact marks that indicate events and scenes.          
Different types of annotation can be represented by different colours or symbols. Some of them might change their appearance regarding the current playback time, e.g. the current chapter can be highlighted.          
The represented annotations on the timeline are used as jump labels providing quick access to the corresponding annotation and content.          
Finally, an annotated timeline supports learners to build a mental model of the time-related and time-dependent information. The timeline symbolizes the temporal layout of the annotated video.          
          
The amount of annotations that can be annotated within the extent of the timeline is limited. It is important that each annotation can be distinguished and selected from each other. Further visualization concepts like filters or clusters (see [Classified Marks](/patterns/view/Classified-Marks)) should be taken into consideration.          
            
The possibility to see the distribution of events over playback time does not explain a single event. Therefore a description should be made available on demand without having to navigate to the temporal position.
context: Enriched videos incorporate time-related contents like chapter marks or tags as well as further contents like pictures, websites or hyperlinks. Their presentation is determined by a temporal layout that contains the position and dimension of these events and marks
forces:
There can be different types of [Annotations](/patterns/view/Annotations), e.g. comments, tags, chapter or section marks, assessments as well as slide or video previews. Some of them refer to a point in time, others to segments of the video. They also overlap each other in a way that multiple annotations relate to the same playback position.            
Some of them can be predefined by the author or publisher, others can be added by users. While the author has the ability to limit the number of own annotations, she or he can not always constrain the extend of user contributions. Beside that the need to map a particular type of annotation depends on the video and the purposed application scenario, e.g. short videos may not need a [Table of Content](/patterns/view/Table-of-Content).
name: Annotated Timeline
problem: The distribution of time-related and time-dependent annotations within the duration of a video is neither visible nor is it possible to navigate precisely to the corresponding positions in time. The learner should have a chance to develop its own mental model on how the interactive video works, and how its temporal events and marks relate to the playback time.
solution: Indicate temporal events and scenes alongside the timeline by different icons, colours or on parallel tracks. Allow users to jump to these temporal positions.
synopsis: Interactive visualization of the temporal layout of events.

In terms of understanding audio, one might not be familiar with the language, the used vocabulary the level of difficulty. Regarding volatile visual content, an object might disappear after a very short time or change their gestalt or look.
solution: Provide a short-cut button to jump back a few seconds back in time in order to repeat the last sentence or the previous scene of the video image.

solution: For editing spread annotations on different timeline tracks. Preserve at least one track for each type of annotation.
synopsis: Use different timeline tracks for editing multiple annotations.

name: Synchronized Maps
context: The content of a video contains many geographic or location-related references. These details are not directly visualized in the video (e.g as a map or an aerial image).
problem: Learners who cannot integrate places or regions mentioned in the video will have difficulties comprehending the contents that are related to these locations.
solution: Show an interactive map beside the video that provides the geographic context. Synchronize the presentation of locations, routes, and areas, but do not restrict the user to navigate the map.
synopsis: Display a synchronized interactive map alongside the video to provide geographic context.
